primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency causing osteopetrosis
mechanism: Carbonic anhydrase II generates intracellular hydrogen ions required for acidification of the osteoclast resorption lacuna. CA2 deficiency impairs osteoclast-mediated mineral dissolution and can also impair renal acidification, producing osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis and intracranial calcification.
vignette: A child has recurrent fractures despite diffusely increased bone density, poor growth, renal tubular acidosis, and intracranial calcifications. Genetic testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function variants in CA2.
lead: Which osteoclast function is most directly impaired?
correct: Generation of hydrogen ions needed to acidify the bone-resorption lacuna
distractors: RANKL-dependent differentiation of monocyte precursors into mature osteoclasts
Cathepsin-K-mediated degradation of type I collagen after mineral dissolution
Attachment of osteoclasts to bone through alpha-v beta-3 integrins
Secretion of osteoprotegerin by osteoblast-lineage cells
distractor_notes: RANKL signaling is required for osteoclast differentiation, but CA2 deficiency produces osteoclast dysfunction rather than a primary failure of osteoclast formation.
Cathepsin K degrades organic collagen matrix after acid-mediated mineral dissolution; CA2 deficiency chiefly blocks the proton-generating step needed for lacunar acidification.
Integrin-mediated attachment is important for creating the sealing zone, but it is not the direct enzymatic consequence of CA2 loss.
Osteoprotegerin is produced by osteoblast-lineage cells and inhibits osteoclastogenesis; it is not an osteoclast carbonic-anhydrase function.
key_expl: Bone resorption requires osteoclasts to acidify the sealed resorption lacuna. Carbonic anhydrase II generates intracellular H+ from CO2 and water, supplying protons for secretion into that compartment. CA2 deficiency therefore impairs mineral dissolution despite the presence of osteoclasts, producing dense but fragile bone and, because CA2 also participates in renal acid handling, renal tubular acidosis.
objective: Explain CA2-deficiency osteopetrosis as failure of osteoclast proton generation and acidification of the bone-resorption lacuna.
